sources.title: The Archaeology of the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Current archaeological synthesis emphasizing regional sequences, local material cultures, subsistence, mobility, burials and the documentary break before empire.

sources.title: Early agropastoral settlement and cultural change in central Tibet in the first millennium BC: excavations at Bangga
sources.note: Excavation, flotation, ceramics, lithics, architecture, crops and fauna at Bangga, with careful comparison to Qugong and Changguogou.

sources.title: Agriculture facilitated permanent human occupation of the Tibetan Plateau after 3600 B.P.
sources.note: Radiocarbon-dated crop and animal evidence linking cold-tolerant barley, wheat and sheep with sustained higher-elevation settlement after about 3600 BP.

sources.title: Early evidence for the use of wheat and barley as staple crops on the margins of the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Direct crop dates and archaeobotanical evidence for changing millet, wheat and barley use on the northeastern plateau margins.

sources.title: Moving agriculture onto the Tibetan plateau: the archaeobotanical evidence
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis of Karuo and Kyung-lung plant evidence, millet beginnings, later barley-wheat-pea systems, caprines and complementary wild foods.

sources.title: A Study on Ancient Barley, Wheat and Millet Discovered at Changguo of Tibet
sources.note: Published identification of naked barley, wheat and foxtail millet at Changguogou in the Yarlung region.

sources.title: Geospatial modelling of farmer to herder interactions maps cultural geography of Bronze and Iron Age Tibet, 3600 to 2200 BP
sources.note: Archaeological distribution and mobility modelling reveal several interaction zones rather than one plateau-wide culture or territory.

sources.title: Radiocarbon chronology and settlement patterns in the Bronze Age of the Qaidam Basin, Northwestern China
sources.note: Radiocarbon, survey, charred crops, grinding tools and fauna support flexible and sometimes mobile agropastoral lifeways in a northeastern basin.

sources.title: Evidence for early domestic yak, taurine cattle, and their hybrids on the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Ancient DNA and zooarchaeology at Bangga identify domestic yak, cattle and hybrids around 2500 BP, alongside caprines, horses, corrals, butchery and dung.

sources.title: Paleoproteomic evidence reveals dairying supported prehistoric occupation of the highland Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Milk proteins in ancient dental calculus, including goat milk at Gepaseru in 1500 to 1312 BCE, document dairy among women, men, adults, children and varied burials.

sources.title: Research reveals the history of dairy consumption among ancient Tibetan Plateau populations
sources.note: Sichuan University archaeological-science account explains dental-calculus paleoproteomics and reports dairy among women, men, adults, children, elites and commoners.

sources.title: The Genome Landscape of Tibetan Sheep Reveals Adaptive Introgression from Argali and the History of Early Human Settlements
sources.note: Sheep genomic history combined with an archaeological site synthesis; useful for livestock dispersal with explicit limits on equating animal genes and human identity.

sources.title: Ancient genomes from the Himalayas illuminate the genetic history of Tibetans and their Tibeto-Burman speaking neighbors
sources.note: Thirty-eight high-altitude individuals include people dated to 1420 BCE and later; ancestry relationships are distinguished from language, culture and modern ethnicity.

sources.title: Human genetic history on the Tibetan Plateau in the past 5100 years
sources.note: Broad ancient-genome transect, radiocarbon control and kinship estimation show continuity plus regional interactions without defining a prehistoric nation.

sources.title: Ancient genomes reveal basal Asian ancestries and dynamic population interactions over time on the southern Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Ancient genomes indicate repeated interaction and admixture on the southern plateau; genetic clusters do not supply names, speech or political boundaries.

sources.title: Altitude adaptation in Tibetans caused by introgression of Denisovan-like DNA
sources.note: EPAS1 study identifies Denisovan-related ancestry involved in present-day Tibetan high-altitude physiology, a deep biological history that cannot label Bronze Age artifacts.

sources.title: Denisovans and Homo sapiens on the Tibetan Plateau: dispersals and adaptations
sources.note: Review separates very ancient hominin occupation, later Homo sapiens settlement, cultural adaptations and genetic selection at altitude.

sources.title: The earliest human occupation of the high-altitude Tibetan Plateau 40 thousand to 30 thousand years ago
sources.note: Excavated stone-tool assemblages at Nwya Devu provide deep background for human use of the plateau, tens of millennia before the atlas interval.

sources.title: Permanent human occupation of the central Tibetan Plateau in the early Holocene
sources.note: Dating of Chusang hand- and footprints demonstrates early central-plateau presence while illustrating chronological debate and method.

sources.title: Middle and Late Pleistocene Denisovan subsistence at Baishiya Karst Cave
sources.note: Zooarchaeology and proteomics reveal Denisovan-related occupation and animal use far earlier than this card; included only as deep regional background.

sources.title: Direct dating of lithic surface artifacts using luminescence
sources.note: Optically stimulated luminescence offers direct burial ages for surface stone artifacts while requiring geomorphic and environmental controls.

sources.title: Foraging and farming: archaeobotanical and zooarchaeological evidence for Neolithic exchange on the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Imported and locally imitated ceramics, plant and animal remains, and varied burials at Zongri demonstrate interaction without simple ethnic equations.

sources.title: On the early metal objects and early Metal Age in Tibet
sources.note: Review of copper, bronze, iron and composite objects argues for a complicated early Metal Age rather than a simple technology-to-people migration story.

sources.title: New Evidence for Prehistoric Textile Production and Social Complexity on the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Spindle whorls, loom evidence and fabric traces from the Yanyuan Basin document household and later socially differentiated textile work.

sources.title: Bioarchaeological profile of stress and dental disease among ancient high altitude Himalayan communities of Nepal
sources.note: Teeth and skeletons reveal site-specific dental disease and stress patterns; the studied communities and dates prevent automatic plateau-wide generalization.

sources.title: Sding Chung: an early multi-burial cave site on the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Excavation of a multi-burial cave emphasizes regional mortuary diversity and limits on reading belief or kinship directly from graves.

sources.title: Mustang: Nepal, for 4,000 years
sources.note: French Ministry of Culture archaeological overview of sparse research, high-mountain routes and second-millennium BCE occupation in Upper Mustang.

sources.title: Cave 17: the Library Cave; the Tibetan annals
sources.note: British Library International Dunhuang Programme dates the earliest surviving Tibetan historical records and Old Tibetan script to the imperial era.

sources.title: The Tibetic Languages: an introduction to the family of languages derived from Old Tibetan
sources.note: CNRS linguistics overview presents Tibetic as a diverse family derived from historically attested Old Tibetan, not a label recoverable from prehistoric pots.

sources.title: Bordering Tibetan Languages
sources.note: Scholarly volume explains literary Tibetan as an imperial-era standard and modern speech diversity, distinguishing language, identity and state projects.

sources.title: Unicode Core Specification: Tibetan
sources.note: Authoritative technical history and structure of Tibetan script; useful for dating the writing tradition far after 500 BCE.

sources.title: Himalayan Region, 500 to 1000 A.D.
sources.note: Metropolitan Museum chronology places the Yarlung state and active Tibetan Buddhist court patronage in the seventh to ninth centuries CE.

sources.title: The Tibetan Plateau on the Eve of Empire
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis places the political formation and written evidence of the Tibetan Empire many centuries after this atlas record.

sources.title: Secrets of Tibetan burial mounds
sources.note: Austrian Academy project on central Tibetan mound landscapes, mostly imperial-era and therefore explicitly used as later contrast.

sources.title: Grasslands of the World: The Tibetan Steppe
sources.note: Institutional ecological overview of cold desert, steppe, meadow, river headwaters, grazing risks and later herding practice; used only for environmental context and labeled comparison.

sources.title: Palaeoenvironmental proxies indicate long-term development of agro-pastoralist landscapes in Inner Asian mountains
sources.note: Pollen, charcoal and other proxies show that mountain agropastoral landscapes developed through long human-environment interaction rather than a single migration.

sources.title: Prehistoric agricultural decision making in the western Himalayas: ecological and social variables
sources.note: Comparative archaeobotany situates Qugong, Changguogou and Bangga mixed cropping after 1500 BCE within high-elevation choices and constraints.

sources.title: The emergence, development, and impact of prehistoric agriculture on the Tibetan plateau
sources.note: Recent synthesis describes successive millet, mixed millet-barley-wheat and barley-wheat systems while emphasizing spatial and chronological variation.

sources.title: The linguistic (pre)history on the eastern Tibetan Plateau: archaeology, palaeoclimate and linguistics
sources.note: Multidisciplinary study models language and archaeological dispersals cautiously and warns that material patterns do not simply identify speech communities.

sources.title: Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan
sources.note: One statistical language-family model linking diversification and early farming; included as a model with uncertainty, never as a direct identification of the atlas population.

sources.title: Tibetan language studies at Oxford
sources.note: University overview distinguishes Central Tibetan, Khams, Amdo and related but separate Tibetic languages, illustrating why the atlas name cannot cover all speakers.

proposedOverrides.summary: A cautious archaeological guide to many plateau communities mapped under an anachronistic “Tibetans” label from 1500 to 500 BCE, with local farming, herding, craft, exchange and high-altitude adaptation kept separate from later empire, script and Buddhism.
